name: 00-intro
title: Nativeproof
subtitle: A real session on nativeproof.vercel.app with live Qloo data and live models
narration: This is Nativeproof, a research workspace for testing how a campaign may be received in another culture before money is spent on it. A team brings a product, a campaign and a target market. Nativeproof finds cultural signals in Qloo's affinity data, rehearses the campaign with a labeled synthetic audience, flags cultural risks, adapts the copy, compares the versions with a fixed scoring rule, and assembles a report in which every claim points back to its source. Everything in this video was recorded on the deployed app on October twenty-ninth, with live Qloo data and live language models. The synthetic participants are generated by AI. They are not real people, and the app says so wherever they appear.

name: d01-architecture
title: How it is built
subtitle: Architecture, deployment and sign-in
narration: First, how the system is built. The web app is Next.js, and it talks to a FastAPI service over HTTPS with a bearer token. Its API types are generated from the service's OpenAPI contract, so the two sides cannot drift apart silently. Inside the API, routes check ownership, a run engine executes long jobs in the background, and each job is a LangGraph workflow with four named stages. Model calls go through one gateway with strict output schemas, while scoring, tallies and rule checks are plain deterministic code. Qloo is reached only from the server, and everything is stored in PostgreSQL.

name: d02-deployment
title: Deployment
narration: In production, the web app runs on Vercel, the API runs on a free Render web service in Singapore, and Supabase provides sign-in, the PostgreSQL database and private file storage. An uptime monitor calls the health endpoint every five minutes, so the free service stays awake. Provider keys exist only as server environment variables. The browser never sees a Qloo key, a model key or a database password.

name: 01-sign-in
title: Sign in
subtitle: Judging account; Google sign-in and an anonymous demo are also available
narration: We sign in with the judging account listed in the README. Google sign-in is on the same page, and Try the demo starts an anonymous session on clearly labeled fixture data, which never calls a live provider. This whole session uses live mode.

name: d03-authentication
title: Authentication
narration: All three sign-in paths end in one Supabase session. The API does not trust the browser: it verifies every token itself against Supabase's public signing keys, checks the expiry, audience and issuer, and uses the token's subject as the user id. Every project belongs to one owner, and a request for another user's data gets a not found response.

name: 02-project
title: Project, brand kit and campaign
subtitle: Every edit creates a new content version
narration: We create a live project for a fictional brand, Trailhead Coffee, which is launching canned cold brew for weekend hikers in Japan. The brand kit records the brand's voice, terms that must stay word for word, and terms that are not allowed. Then we add the campaign copy and the cultural references we want to investigate. Every edit creates a new, immutable content version, so each later result names exactly which copy it tested.

name: d04-lifecycle
title: The research workflow
subtitle: From a project to an evidence-backed report
narration: This is the path a campaign takes. Atlas discovers cultural evidence for a market. Audience rehearses the campaign with synthetic participants. Voice writes market adaptations, Loop evaluates the original against the candidates under one scoring version, and Proof assembles the report. Brand Memory is written only by people and is read by every step.

name: d05-qloo
title: Qloo evidence pipeline
narration: Here is how a Qloo result becomes evidence. Inputs are validated, and terms that look like an email address or a phone number are refused before anything leaves the server. Only an allowlist of workflows can run. Each response is normalized into evidence records that keep the retrieval mode, the retrieval time and hashes of the request and response, and live results are cached for a limited time. When a term matches several candidates, nothing is chosen automatically.

name: 03-atlas
title: Atlas: Qloo evidence
subtitle: Ambiguous matches are confirmed by a person, never guessed
narration: Atlas resolves the campaign's concepts against Qloo. In this live run, all five terms came back ambiguous. Qloo holds several tags named Hiking, for example as a hobby, an activity and a lifestyle. Nativeproof does not guess. It lists the candidates, and we confirm the intended one with Use this. Each choice reruns discovery, and each run took between thirty and sixty-six seconds. With all five confirmed, ten signals resolved. The market brief keeps source data apart from model interpretation, every finding cites its evidence, and its risks state plainly that affinity data does not prove demand.

name: 04-rehearsal
title: Quick rehearsal
subtitle: A study with research questions, grounded in discovery evidence
narration: A population study builds on a study, so we create one with two research questions and run the quick rehearsal first. It generated twelve synthetic reactions grounded in ten discovery evidence records, in fifty-six seconds. It already raised something we had not considered: several reactions were unsure how hikers would carry the can and dispose of it on the trail.

name: d07-population
title: How a synthetic population is built
subtitle: Groups from evidence, participants from groups, interviews in batches
narration: A population study works in three steps. A model proposes audience groups, and each group must cite the Qloo evidence it is built from. Participants are then sampled into those groups with a fixed random seed, so the same population can be interviewed again later. Interviews run in batches, and every completed batch is saved as a checkpoint before the next one starts.

name: 05-population-start
title: Population study: 100 participants
subtitle: Background run with checkpoints, cancel and resume
narration: Now the main study. We build a new synthetic population of one hundred participants for Japan at standard interview depth, and we upload the ad creative, so participants react to what a vision model actually observes in the image, not to a guess about it. The study runs in the background, reports its stage and batch, and can be cancelled or resumed.

name: 06-population-results
title: Population results
subtitle: Deterministic tallies of stored interviews
narration: The study finished in two minutes and twenty seconds, and all one hundred interviews completed. Seventy-one percent were positive, twelve percent mixed and seventeen percent neutral, with none negative or confused. The participants come from four groups built from the Qloo evidence, twenty-five in each. Every number here is a tally of stored interviews, not a model's estimate, and the recommendations name their own gaps, such as the absence of negative voices.

name: 24-population-browse
title: Reaction graph and interviews
subtitle: Every interview is labeled as AI-generated
narration: The reaction graph links the campaign's elements to the groups, their reactions and the themes they raised. Each edge carries a stored count and a definition of what the count means, and selecting a node highlights its links. Below, every interview can be read in full: the participant's group, reaction and comprehension, each answer to the eight questions, and the label that says it is an AI-generated reaction, not a real participant.

name: d09-social
title: How the social simulation works
subtitle: Rounds, feeds, stances and traceable influence
narration: The social simulation runs in rounds. In each round, a share of participants reads a feed of peer posts and interviews, chosen with a fixed seed, and then posts, comments, shares or ignores. Each action stores the stance before and after, the stated reason, and the exact feed items the participant saw. That is what makes every claimed influence traceable, and each completed round is a checkpoint.

name: 07-social-simulation
title: Multi-round social simulation
subtitle: Stance changes with reasons and the posts that caused them
narration: We run three rounds. In each one, twenty percent of the participants read a feed of five peer items, then act. The simulation completed in seventy seconds, with nine, four and eight stance changes across the rounds. Each post shows the stance before and after, the participant's reason, and the posts it reacted to.

name: 25-diffusion
title: Social diffusion graph
subtitle: Which groups' posts and interviews reached which groups, round by round
narration: The diffusion graph shows how content moved. Each arrow from one audience group to another counts the feed items written by the first group that were shown to the second in this round, and thicker lines carry more items. Earlier-round posts and the participants' interviews appear as sources too. Selecting a group highlights its links, and the panel lists each connection with its count, its definition and the stored field it comes from. The view is labeled illustrative. It is not a forecast of real reach.

name: d08-interviews
title: Interviews, memory and follow-ups
subtitle: Answers cite stored memories and become memories
narration: Participants keep a memory of what they said and saw. A follow-up question is answered from those stored memories, the answer must cite which memories it used, and it is saved as a new memory. Questions to a whole group go to a seeded sample, and the tally covers only that sample.

name: 08-follow-ups
title: Participant memory and follow-ups
subtitle: Answers cite stored memories and become memories
narration: This participant's current stance comes from round one, and its memories are its interview and its own post. We ask a follow-up about carrying the empty can back down the mountain. The answer cites one stored memory and is saved as a new memory. We can also question a whole group: a seeded sample of five answered, and the tally covers only those five.

name: d06-gateway
title: The model gateway
subtitle: One place for routing, validation, retries and usage
narration: Every model call goes through one gateway. Each task has a configured model and a minimum capability, and outputs must match a strict schema. Invalid output gets a bounded repair attempt, provider errors get bounded retries, and a fallback provider is used only when it is enabled and capable. Usage and latency are recorded per stage, which is how the report can list the model and prompt version behind every step.

name: 10-risk-radar
title: Risk Radar with vision
subtitle: Observations kept apart from interpretations
narration: Risk Radar scans the copy and the image together. A vision model, MiniCPM-V, analyzed the uploaded creative. In twenty-seven seconds the scan found five potential issues, one moderate and four low. The moderate one is the line, crack one open at the summit, which the model reads as a possible clash with etiquette at sacred peaks in Japan. The quoted text is checked against the copy in code, and the reading is labeled as model interpretation. Applying the suggested change creates a new adaptation; the campaign is never edited in place.

name: 11-voice
title: Voice adaptations
subtitle: Every change shows what it replaces and why
narration: Voice writes market adaptations, grounded in the discovery evidence and the rehearsal findings. It produced two variants in about fifteen seconds. Each change shows what it replaces, why, and whether evidence supports it, and deterministic checks confirm that protected terms were kept and prohibited terms were avoided.

name: 12-loop-evaluation
title: Loop evaluation
subtitle: Deterministic decision rules, no invented winner
narration: Loop scores the original and three candidates under one scoring version, from synthetic ratings on clarity, brand fit, cultural relevance and risk. The best candidate scored ninety point five against eighty-five point eight for the original. Because the margin is under five points, the decision rule recommends validating with real people instead of declaring a winner.

name: 13-version-comparison
title: Versions on identical participants
subtitle: Same 100-person population, version 2 against version 3
narration: Loop can also compare versions on identical participants. We saved the risk fix as version three and interviewed the same one hundred participants again. Reusing the population skipped all Qloo and construction work. The result is honest: positive reactions fell from seventy-one to sixty-six percent. The fix may remove a cultural risk but cost some emotional pull, and the app states that no statistical significance is claimed.

name: d12-runs
title: Runs, checkpoints and recovery
subtitle: What happens when a run is cancelled or the server restarts
narration: Long work runs in the background with a clear lifecycle: queued, running, then completed, partial, failed or cancelled. Population studies and social simulations save a checkpoint after every batch or round. Cancelling stops at the next checkpoint and keeps the finished work. If the server restarts, a startup sweep marks unfinished runs as interrupted, and runs with a checkpoint can be resumed from where they stopped.

name: 21-cancel
title: Cancel
subtitle: A run stops at a checkpoint and keeps its finished work
narration: Here we start another study on the same population and cancel it after the first batch. It stops at the next checkpoint and keeps what was finished: forty of one hundred interviews, saved and readable. A cancelled run is final, because the person chose to stop it.

name: 27-resume
title: Resume after a server restart
subtitle: A real restart of the production API in the middle of a study
narration: Resume is for runs that a restart interrupted, and this is a real one. We start a study on the same population, and twelve seconds later we restart the production API on Render. The new server's startup sweep finds the study unfinished and marks it interrupted. The page says the server restarted during the run, that completed work is saved, and offers Resume from last checkpoint. Eighty-one interviews were saved; nine that were in progress when the old server shut down are recorded as failed. We resume. The run continues from its checkpoint instead of starting over, and finishes with ninety-one completed interviews. The nine failed ones are named and excluded from every tally, rather than quietly filled in.

name: 18-arena
title: Campaign Arena
subtitle: Concepts side by side for one audience and one set of criteria
narration: Campaign Arena puts concepts side by side for the same synthetic audience and the same criteria. In eighty seconds, variant B led with ninety-three point eight out of a hundred, and the original was marked as within five points of the leader, so the result is close and is shown that way.

name: 16-cultural-dna
title: Cultural DNA
subtitle: A versioned profile where every item cites evidence
narration: Cultural DNA turns the discovery evidence into a versioned cultural profile in under thirty seconds. Every item cites its Qloo source, items without support are labeled as hypotheses, and conflicts between signals are listed instead of smoothed over.

name: 28-market-expansion
title: Market Expansion
subtitle: The same discovery across markets, with ambiguous terms confirmed once
narration: Market Expansion runs the same discovery in two to five markets and lays the evidence side by side. We compare Japan and South Korea for canned cold brew coffee, with the terms hiking and cold brew coffee. All three terms come back ambiguous, so at first both markets are unavailable. The ambiguous terms are listed once, above the markets, with the same Use this buttons as Atlas. Qloo's tag matching does not depend on the market, so one confirmation applies to every market, and the comparison runs again with it. We confirm hiking as an activity, and both markets complete. Then we confirm cold brew coffee, and each market shows four resolved signals with opportunities, risks and gaps, while the product category, which we left unconfirmed, stays listed. The page records the matches we confirmed. The signals are identical in both markets, so the page says plainly that they cannot rank the markets.

name: 19-brand-trend
title: Brand Memory and Trend Watch
subtitle: Rules every workflow reads; snapshots compared deterministically
narration: Brand Memory stores the rules every workflow reads, such as the voice and the protected and prohibited terms. Trend Watch compares two saved discovery snapshots without calling a model. It shows which signals appeared and disappeared, and it warns that two snapshots are not a trend line, and that a difference can come from matching changes rather than from culture.

name: d10-database
title: Where the evidence lives
subtitle: The data model and the evidence graph
narration: Every result is stored in PostgreSQL with explicit relationships: projects own campaigns, campaigns own immutable content versions, runs record their inputs and stages, and evidence records keep their source, type and retrieval details. Schema changes go through migrations, and row level security protects user-owned tables.

name: d11-evidence-graph
title: Evidence Graph
narration: The Evidence Graph is built only from those stored links. Every edge names the stored field that establishes it. A link that was never recorded is never inferred, and large graphs return a bounded subgraph that says it was truncated.

name: 29-evidence-graph
title: Evidence Graph
subtitle: Only stored links are drawn
narration: Here is the graph for this session. Zoomed in, each line is a stored link: a run produced an evidence record, the evidence supports an adaptation, an evaluation evaluates a version. Selecting a node highlights its connections and lists each one with the field it comes from. This node is a Qloo source signal produced by a discovery run, with its retrieval details and limitations attached.

name: 30-search
title: Project search
subtitle: Semantic search over stored evidence and findings
narration: Ctrl K opens project search. It is semantic search over the project's stored evidence, risk findings, Cultural DNA items, adaptations and brand examples. Each hit shows its type and evidence label, and the similarity score is described as a ranking signal, not a probability. Opening an evidence hit shows the full record.

name: 15-proof-report
title: Proof report
subtitle: Assembled from stored results, with reproducibility details
narration: Finally, Proof assembles the report in thirteen seconds without calling a model. It carries the verdict, the evidence register, the limitations, the validation steps, and a reproducibility section with model identifiers, prompt versions and each stage's provider and latency. It exports as Markdown or JSON, or prints to PDF.

name: 20-home
title: Home dashboard
subtitle: Counts of stored records across the account
narration: Back on Home, the dashboard counts what this session produced: the project, the market researched, the evidence records and the recent completed runs. Each number is a count of stored records, not an estimate.

name: 99-outro
title: Validate with real people
subtitle: github.com/vishavmehra/NativeProof
narration: Nativeproof helps teams find cultural risks and opportunities before launch, and it says clearly when the evidence is not enough. Every claim is labeled as source data, calculation, interpretation or hypothesis, and synthetic participants are a tool for forming hypotheses, not for proving them. Decisions still need validation with real people. The code, the twelve diagrams and the setup guide are on GitHub.
